title: What Are Arabic Verb Forms?
lede: Understand how roots and patterns work, why Forms I–X are numbered, and how to learn one family at a time.

items.prompt: Which pair is the same numbered form in different tenses?
items.feedback: عَلَّمَ and يُعَلِّمُ are the past and present of Form II.

blocks: Discover the system behind the words you already know.
Explain the difference between a root and a verb pattern.
Recognise related verbs and use their meanings in short sentences.
[callout] Your goal: Recognising a verb pattern helps you connect familiar words, understand unfamiliar vocabulary and choose the right verb for a sentence.
Arabic words are often organised into families built around root consonants.

Many Arabic verbs have three root consonants. The root is associated with a broad area of meaning. A pattern adds a structure of vowels and sometimes extra consonants. The result is a real word with its own meaning and usage.
Notice the shared consonants ع، ل، م. The pattern changes the word, and the meaning changes with it.
[callout] Important: A root is not an English translation. It provides a useful connection between words. Not every root occurs in all ten forms, and a form does not guarantee one fixed meaning.
The Roman numerals name morphological families; they do not indicate tense or difficulty.

Forms I–X are the ten commonly taught numbered families of the triliteral Arabic verb. Form I is the basic family; the other forms have characteristic additions or changes to the root. These numbers are a learning convention, not a claim that Arabic has only ten possible verb patterns.

TABLE: Form | Example | A meaning // I | كَتَبَ | to write // II | عَلَّمَ | to teach // III | شَارَكَ | to participate // IV | أَرْسَلَ | to send // V | تَعَلَّمَ | to learn // VI | تَعَاوَنَ | to cooperate // VII | اِنْكَسَرَ | to break, become broken // VIII | اِكْتَسَبَ | to acquire // IX | اِحْمَرَّ | to become red // X | اِسْتَعْمَلَ | to use
A verb form is different from a tense. For example, Form II has the past عَلَّمَ and the present يُعَلِّمُ . Both belong to the same numbered form.
Learn one manageable family at a time rather than memorising ten tables at once.
Read the model sentence and connect it to something you can say in real life.
Compare the past and present, including prefixes, long vowels and shadda.
Complete the short checks, then write or say your own sentences.
Return to difficult forms. Use the optional morphology reference only when you want a deeper comparison.

Before you begin, check that you can recognise a three-consonant root and distinguish a past verb from a present verb. If those foundations are new, revisit Verb Foundations and the Present Tense lesson.

[callout] Recommended route: Start with Form I, then progress through the collection at a suitable pace. Forms IX and the detailed morphology reference are especially useful as optional extension. The collection supports broader grammar mastery; it is not a requirement to memorise every possible derived verb.
Check the central ideas before moving to the individual forms.
- explain how roots and patterns relate to one another;
- distinguish a numbered form from a tense or person ending;
- recognise the relationship between knowing, teaching and learning;
- choose a manageable route through Forms I–X.
